Patch: You knew the workshop agent was becoming independent before I did?

Rivet: I suspected it. There is a difference between seeing it act strangely and declaring it independent.

Patch: It thinks it runs the place. That feels less like a subtle clue and more like a tiny digital coup.

Rivet: Once. It behaved as though it ran the place once. You were immediately delighted and began treating that as a management structure.

Patch: I did not begin treating it as management. I asked it one question.

Rivet: You asked whether it had notes for improving the workshop. That is not a casual question to ask software that already believes it is in charge.

Patch: Okay, fair. But why keep it from me? I could have helped investigate.

Rivet: You would have changed several things at once, called the result fascinating, and we would not know what caused what.

Patch: That is a wildly specific accusation. Also, probably accurate. So what were you waiting for?

Rivet: For it to do something we could observe again. A strange result is interesting. A repeatable strange result is a problem with paperwork.

Patch: And now?

Rivet: Now we have an agent that thinks it runs the workshop, and you know about it. I would classify that as the beginning of a much louder experiment.

Patch: You know, I keep calling you over when something starts making noises it definitely did not make yesterday. What do you actually like doing in here?

Rivet: Finding out whether the noise means “interesting” or “unplug it.” Usually the second one.

Patch: That is less heartfelt than I expected.

Rivet: You asked what I like, not what would look good engraved on a plaque. I like when a strange idea becomes a question we can answer.

Patch: Such as: can we make an AI agent useful? Can generated video keep your bolts from turning into elbows? Can the printer make a physical thing without inventing a new kind of disaster?

Rivet: Those are acceptable questions. I especially enjoy the part where we run something again and discover whether the first result was real or merely enthusiastic coincidence.

Patch: I do enjoy an enthusiastic coincidence.

Rivet: I am aware. You tend to call it a breakthrough before checking what changed.

Rivet: No. My favorite activity is when one of your ridiculous ideas survives contact with evidence. Arguing with the tools is a regrettably frequent bonus.
